title: How to Tell If an Award Redemption Is Actually Worth It
summary: How to tell if an award redemption is worth it: calculate cents per point after fees, compare it to what your points are worth elsewhere, and spot bad deals.
body_markdown:
A business class award that "saves" you $4,000 can still be a worse use of your points than a $650 economy seat. It depends on four questions that are easy to skip.


Award prices are easy to mistake for bargains. A points price next to a big cash fare makes any redemption feel like a win, but the points price leaves out the taxes still to come and says nothing about the trip those points could have paid for instead or the fact that a transfer cannot be undone.


This guide gives you one test to run on any award price before you move a single point. It works for economy and first class, for a short domestic hop or a trip across the world, and it takes about two minutes once you know the four questions.


At Pointhound, every search shows the points price and which program books the seat. This is what to do with that result before you commit.


## What Does Cents Per Point Mean?


Cents per point is the cash value a redemption gives you for each point you spend, and it is the number every other step compares against.


Here is the formula, including the step that is easiest to skip:


> **Cents per point = (cash price - taxes and fees on the award) / points needed x 100**


The subtraction matters. An award is rarely paid in points alone. Virgin Atlantic, for example, shows its reward seat prices "plus applicable taxes, fees and charges" ([Virgin Atlantic](https://www.virginatlantic.com/en-US/flying-club/spend-points/reward-seats/saver-reward-seats) ). You pay those fees in cash either way, so they are not part of what your points bought.


A quick example. If a flight costs $500 in cash, and the award costs 25,000 points plus $50 in fees, your points bought $450 of travel. That is 1.8 cents per point.


On its own, 1.8 means nothing. It only becomes a good or bad number once you know what those same points could do somewhere else, which is where the test comes in.


## The Four-Question Redemption Test


The four-question redemption test checks an award price against what you would really pay, what the award really costs, what your points are worth elsewhere, and what happens if plans change.


Question What to check The trap it catches


1. What would you actually pay in cash? The ticket you would have bought, not the priciest one Valuing a seat you would never pay for


2. What does the award really cost? Points plus taxes, fees and carrier-imposed charges Treating an award as free


3. What are these points worth elsewhere? Your floor value and a published valuation Spending points below their value


4. What happens if your plans change? Transfer rules and award cancellation rules Locking points into one airline


### 1. What would you actually pay in cash?


The cash price that counts is the ticket you would have bought, not the most expensive seat on the route.


If you would never pay $4,000 for business class, using $4,000 in the formula inflates the result. Use what the trip is worth to you: the economy fare you would otherwise have booked, or the most you would honestly pay for the upgrade.


No other question does as much to keep a flashy number honest.


### 2. What does the award really cost?


The award costs its points plus every dollar of taxes, fees and carrier-imposed charges, and those vary more than most beginners expect.


On partner flights booked through Alaska's Atmos Rewards, taxes and carrier-imposed fees start from **$5.60 per person each way** , and since July 1, 2026 a non-refundable $20 partner award fee applies on top ([Alaska Airlines](https://www.alaskaair.com/atmosrewards/content/use-points/award-charts) ). Leave from London and fees jump. From April 1, 2026, UK Air Passenger Duty on a flight to the United States is £102 in the lowest class of travel and £244 in any other class ([GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/rates-and-allowances-for-air-passenger-duty) ).


That duty is only one line of the bill. Airlines can add their own charges on top, so read the full total on the booking page before you compare anything.


### 3. What are these points worth somewhere else?


Your points are worth whatever else they could do, so compare every award against two benchmarks: a floor and a published valuation.


The **floor** is what your points get with no effort at all. American Express says its points are worth 1 cent each on flights booked through Amex Travel, but only 0.6 cents as a statement credit ([American Express](https://www.americanexpress.com/en-us/credit-cards/credit-intel/american-express-points-value/) ). Chase's Points Boost can make some cardmembers' points worth "up to 2x" their usual value on select flights booked through Chase Travel ([Chase](https://www.chase.com/travel/guide/trips/chase-sapphire-points-boost-benefits-guide) ). Our guide to[the credit card portal versus transferring points](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/credit-card-portal-vs-transferring-points) covers that choice in depth.


The **valuation** is a published estimate of what a currency is typically worth. Here are The Points Guy's September 2026 figures ([The Points Guy](https://thepointsguy.com/loyalty-programs/monthly-valuations/) ):


Points currency Valuation (cents per point)


Bilt 2.2


Chase Ultimate Rewards 2.05


Amex Membership Rewards 2.0


Citi ThankYou Rewards 1.9


Capital One 1.85


Alaska Atmos Rewards 1.55


Air Canada Aeroplan 1.5


Virgin Atlantic Flying Club 1.45


Air France-KLM Flying Blue 1.4


United MileagePlus 1.2


Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles 1.1


Every card currency on TPG's list is valued above every airline currency on it. That fits how transfers work: card points can still move to several airlines, but once transferred, they are worth only what that one airline decides.


TPG itself calls these "estimates" and says the value you actually get "may be higher or lower depending on your goals, flexibility" and how you use them. Treat a valuation as a bar to clear, not a price tag.


### 4. What happens if your plans change?


If plans change, what you lose depends on whether points already left your card account, because transfers are one way.


Chase puts it plainly: "Keep in mind that point transfers to travel partners are final" ([Chase](https://www.chase.com/personal/credit-cards/education/basics/how-to-transfer-chase-ultimate-rewards-points) ). Once points sit in an airline program, that airline's rules and future prices govern them.


The award ticket itself can be more forgiving. Atmos Rewards says it refunds your points and any taxes paid if you cancel an award before departure, subject to its terms, though the $20 partner award fee is non-refundable ([Alaska Airlines](https://www.alaskaair.com/atmosrewards/content/use-points/award-charts) ). Rules differ by program, so check before you book, not after. Our[guide to transferring credit card points to airlines](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/how-to-transfer-credit-card-points-to-airlines) covers the transfer side.


One more cost hides here. A cash ticket usually earns airline miles. Award bookings can sometimes earn miles too, but that varies by program. On Atmos Rewards award flights, you earn 1 status point toward elite status for every mile flown ([Alaska Airlines](https://www.alaskaair.com/atmosrewards/content/use-points/award-charts) ).


## Three Worked Examples


The same test gives three very different verdicts depending on the fare, the fees and which points get you there.


The award prices below are the programs' published starting prices. The cash fares and fee totals are illustrations, so swap in the numbers from your own search.


Redemption Points Fees (illustration) Cash fare (illustration) Cents per point Verdict


London to New York, Virgin Atlantic Saver economy 6,000 $330 $650 5.3 Strong


London to New York, Virgin Atlantic Upper Class 29,000 $970 $4,000 10.4 on paper Depends on question 1


Short Atmos partner flight under 700 miles 4,500 $25.60 $89 1.4 Usually pay cash


### Example A: economy to New York for 6,000 points


Virgin Atlantic's Saver seats from London to New York start at **6,000 points** in economy ([Virgin Atlantic](https://www.virginatlantic.com/en-US/flying-club/spend-points/reward-seats/saver-reward-seats) ). Say the cash fare is $650 and the award shows $330 in taxes, fees and charges, £102 of it UK Air Passenger Duty.


Your points bought $320 of travel, or 5.3 cents per point. That clears every valuation in the table by a wide margin, and all five major card programs reach Virgin Atlantic, Capital One through its Virgin Red partnership ([Virgin Red](https://www.virgin.com/en-us/virgin-red/capital-one) ). Run question 4, confirm the seat is open, and this is a strong use of points.


### Example B: Upper Class on the same route


Upper Class, Virgin's lie-flat business cabin, starts at 29,000 points one way on the same route. Say the cash fare is $4,000 and the fees total $970, including £244 of Air Passenger Duty. On paper, that is 10.4 cents per point.


Now run question 1. If you would have flown economy anyway, the real question is what the bed is worth to you. Compared with Example A, the upgrade costs 23,000 more points and about $640 more in fees. Valued at roughly 2 cents per card point, TPG's ballpark for the major card currencies, that is around $1,100 for a lie-flat seat across the Atlantic.


For many travelers that is a great trade, and it is why[cheap business class with points](https://www.pointhound.com/blog/how-to-find-cheap-business-class-flights-with-points) gets so much attention. For others, the 23,000 points pay for a second economy trip. Both answers pass the test. Only you can run question 1.


### Example C: a short flight for 4,500 points


Atmos Rewards partner flights under 700 miles in the Americas start at **4,500 points** . The cash side starts at $25.60: taxes from $5.60 plus the $20 partner award fee ([Alaska Airlines](https://www.alaskaair.com/atmosrewards/content/use-points/award-charts) ). Say the cash fare is $89. Your points bought about $63 of travel, or 1.4 cents per point.


That beats a 1-cent floor like Amex's, which makes it look like a win. But Bilt is the only one of the five major card programs that transfers to Atmos Rewards, and 1.4 cents falls short of TPG's estimate for every card currency in the table, not just Bilt's. It even trails TPG's 1.55-cent estimate for Atmos points, and the cash ticket would usually earn miles of its own. If you already hold Atmos points, it is a close call. If you would be transferring Bilt points, the test points to paying cash and saving them for a bigger redemption.


## When Is a High Cents Per Point Still a Bad Deal?


A high cents per point is still a bad deal when it measures a price you would never pay, ignores fees, or spends points you need for a harder trip.


Watch for four situations:


- **The cash price is fiction.** A $12,000 first class fare makes any award look incredible. If you would never have paid it, the number flatters you.
- **The fees swallow the savings.** On a cheap fare, a large fee total can leave your points buying very little. Run question 2 before you celebrate.
- **The points had a better job.** Points spent on a decent redemption today are not available for the trip where they would have been worth three times as much.
- **The plan is shaky.** If a trip may not happen, a final transfer into one airline turns flexible points into miles you may struggle to use.


None of these mean avoid premium cabins. Premium awards are where points stretch furthest, roughly 10x portal value in business class and up to 20x in first. They mean run the test honestly on the fare in front of you.


## How to Run the Test in Two Minutes


Running the test takes five steps, and the transfer comes last.


1. **Find the points price and which program books the seat.** One Pointhound search checks 21 loyalty programs and 200+ airlines, shows the points price on every result, and includes step-by-step booking instructions.
2. **Note the cash fare you would really pay** for the same trip.
3. **Read the full fee total** on the airline's booking page.
4. **Do the math** and compare the result with your floor and the valuation of the points you would transfer.
5. **Check the change and cancellation rules** , then transfer and book directly with the airline.


Most transfers are instant, though some take longer, so check the timing and move points only when you are ready to book. Pointhound is a search and discovery tool, and you always book directly with the airline.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is a good cents per point value?


A good value is one that clearly beats what your points could do elsewhere. The Points Guy's September 2026 estimates put major card currencies between 1.85 and 2.2 cents per point, and Amex says its points are worth 1 cent on flights through Amex Travel. Treat both as bars to clear.


### Should I subtract taxes and fees when calculating cents per point?


Yes. You pay taxes, fees and carrier-imposed charges in cash on most awards, so they are not part of what your points bought. Subtract them from the cash fare before dividing by the points. Skipping this step makes awards from high-fee airports look far better than they are.


### Is it better to use points or pay cash for cheap flights?


Often it is better to pay cash. On a cheap fare, the value per point can fall below what the same points are worth elsewhere, and a cash ticket usually earns airline miles. Save points for fares where the value per point clearly beats your benchmark, which is most common in premium cabins.


### Why do points valuations differ between sources?


Valuations are estimates, and each publisher weighs award prices, fees, availability and redemption data differently. The Points Guy says the value you actually get may be higher or lower depending on your goals and flexibility. Use any valuation as a benchmark, and trust the math on your own fare more.


### Do award flights earn miles?


Sometimes. Award bookings can sometimes earn miles, depending on the program, while a cash ticket usually earns them. On Atmos Rewards award flights, you earn 1 status point toward elite status for every mile flown. Factor the miles a cash ticket would earn into your decision when the value per point is close.


## Key Takeaways


- Cents per point is the cash price minus award taxes and fees, divided by the points needed, times 100.
- The four-question redemption test checks what you would really pay, what the award really costs, what your points are worth elsewhere, and what happens if plans change.
- UK Air Passenger Duty adds £102 in economy and £244 in other cabins to flights from most UK airports to the U.S. from April 1, 2026, before any airline charges.
- The Points Guy's September 2026 estimates put major card currencies at 1.85 to 2.2 cents per point, above every airline currency on its list.
- A short-haul award that beats a 1-cent floor can still be the wrong call if it falls below published valuations for the points you would transfer, especially once partner award fees are added.
- Point transfers are final, so run the test before moving anything.


## A Good Redemption Is One You Checked


There is no universal good number, only a good number for your fare, your points and your plans. Run the four questions and most bad redemptions reveal themselves in under two minutes.
